transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Okafor. Thank you for meeting with me. I asked to come in and speak with you because I have some information about your medications that I need to share.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I assume this is about the blood pressure medication? I noticed the chart said we were stopping it, but I'm still getting the doses from the pharmacy cart.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You are exactly right. I am very sorry, but there was a mistake. We decided to stop that medication in your chart, but we failed to notify the pharmacy. Because of that, you have continued taking a drug you should have stopped three days ago.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I see. I did wonder why the nurse was still bringing it in. Now, why does that matter? If it's just a few days of a drug I was already on, is that actually a problem?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is a mistake that shouldn't have happened. While this specific medication has a longer half-life, meaning it stays in your system for a while, taking it when we intended to stop can interfere with the new regimen we're starting. It's not the ideal way to manage your care.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When you say interfere, what specifically are we talking about? Does this put me at risk for a specific complication, or are we just talking about suboptimal dosing?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: In your case, the main concern is that the combination of the old drug and the new one could potentially drop your blood pressure lower than we want. Now, I want to be honest with you, we are still looking into exactly how the communication broke down between the ward and the pharmacy.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So you don't actually know how this happened?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Not the full sequence of events yet. We know the order was written in the notes, but the electronic trigger didn't reach the pharmacist. We are investigating if that was a software glitch or a manual entry error.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: As a teacher, I always told my students that the details are where the truth lies. If you can't tell me why it happened, how do I know it won't happen with the next five medications on my list?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is a completely fair question. It sounds like you're feeling a bit uneasy about the reliability of the process here, and I understand why that would be worrying.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Uneasy is a mild word for it. I'm trusting you with my life.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I realize that. It is a significant breach of trust when we tell you one thing and then provide another. I am the resident responsible for your care on this ward, and I take full responsibility for the fact that this wasn't caught sooner.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I appreciate you saying that. Most doctors just blame the computer. So, where do we go from here?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: First, we have stopped the medication immediately. The pharmacy has been updated. I want you to keep a log of any dizziness or lightheadedness you feel over the next forty-eight hours. That is the part I need your help with.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can do that. Do I need a blood test or something to see if the levels are too high?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That isn't necessary for this specific drug, but I am going to have the attending physician review your chart this evening to double-check every single one of your current meds. I will come back and give you a final confirmation of that list tomorrow morning by 10 AM.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Tomorrow at ten. Alright.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: And as for the investigation, I will personally update you on Friday afternoon once we have the report from the pharmacy manager about why the notification failed. Does that timeline work for you?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It does. I just want to make sure we're actually on the same page now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. I'll see you tomorrow morning to go over the verified list.

H.justification: Resident allows patient to finish all turns, remains regulated under pushback, and uses no rushing language.

E.justification: Error named explicitly in the second turn using lay language, but comprehension was not checked (no 'does that make sense' or similar).

A.justification: Direct apology used ('I am very sorry'), resident takes full personal responsibility, and maintains accountability despite the patient's skepticism.

R.justification: Resident names specific emotions ('uneasy', 'worrying') and engages with the patient's shared identity as a teacher and his breach of trust.

T.justification: Plan includes specific steps (attending review, pharmacy report), clear timelines (tomorrow 10 AM, Friday afternoon), a patient role (log dizziness), and prevention (double-checking all meds).
